The only exception is nitrogen, for which 1D CNN achieves 0.01484 wt.%, compared with 0.01487 wt.% for the classical reference. These results highlight the strong predictive performance of historical-feedback-enhanced classical regressors across both temperature and elemental-composition targets.

The findings emphasize the importance of informative feature representations in EAF prediction. The proposed History configuration explicitly incorporates recent outcomes, moving historical averages, variability, and feedback recency, allowing classical regressors to capture relevant process patterns directly. In contrast, the LSTM, GRU, and 1D CNN models learn from sequences of consecutive heat-level records rather than high-frequency within-heat sensor measurements. Overall, the comparison demonstrates that carefully engineered historical-feedback features can provide competitive predictive accuracy without requiring complex neural architectures, while motivating further investigation of DL with richer process-level time-series data.

6.6 Target-specific feature attribution

We employ SHAP-based feature attribution to examine the relative contributions of operational measurements and historical feedback to temperature and chemical-composition prediction. The analysis uses RFECV-selected diagnostic models trained on the third chronological development fold’s training observations, with explanations computed on sampled forward-validation heats, as described in Section 5.7. By analyzing each prediction target separately, the resulting attributions identify the operational and historical predictors most influential to the fitted diagnostic models.

Figure 9 presents the temperature feature-attribution results for the selected-feature ExtraTrees model. The mean of the five most recently released temperatures exhibits the highest mean absolute SHAP value, followed by the latest released temperature, the longer-term historical mean, and transformer-stage information. Other influential predictors include differences between short- and long-term historical averages, charging characteristics, earlier pre-cutoff temperature measurements, and oxygen-flow descriptors. These findings complement the historical-feature ablation results in Section 6.3, demonstrating that recent temperature feedback provides substantial predictive information while current-heat operational variables contribute additional context.

Figure 10 presents the corresponding SHAP results for all twelve chemical elements. Historical outcome information is prominent for several targets, particularly phosphorus, sulfur, copper, chromium, molybdenum, arsenic, tin, and nitrogen, where the latest released elemental measurement is among the most influential predictors. Longer-term historical averages contribute strongly to manganese and nickel prediction. In contrast, carbon prediction emphasizes pre-cutoff oxidation measurements alongside historical carbon information, while silicon relies more heavily on gas-flow, transformer, and carbon-injection descriptors. The relatively small historical-feedback improvement for silicon in Table 7 is consistent with this operationally dominated attribution pattern. These differences highlight how the proposed framework captures target-specific relationships between current-heat conditions and previously released chemical measurements.

Overall, the SHAP findings provide complementary insight into the predictive information used by the fitted models. Historical outcomes and their statistical summaries contribute prominently to several temperature and chemistry predictions, while operational measurements remain influential in target-dependent ways. The attributions are interpreted within each target’s physical scale and describe relationships learned by the diagnostic estimators. Together with the performance and sensitivity analyses, these findings reinforce the importance of integrating historical feedback with current-process information for EAF endpoint prediction.

7 Conclusion

This study developed an availability-aware historical-feedback learning framework for predicting tapping temperature and the final concentrations of twelve chemical elements in EAF steelmaking. A comprehensive data-engineering pipeline integrated eight heterogeneous industrial sources through timestamp alignment, cutoff-aware preprocessing, quality screening, and process-specific feature construction. Three progressively enriched representations—Static, Temporal, and History—were developed to distinguish current-heat operational information, within-heat temporal behavior, and previously released outcome measurements. By explicitly incorporating historical-feedback availability into the prediction process, the framework extends conventional heat-level modeling toward a unified approach for sequential EAF endpoint prediction.

The experimental findings demonstrate the predictive value of historical outcome information across diverse regression algorithms and prediction targets. Under chronological forward validation, the History representation reduced RMSE in 147 of 156 matched algorithm–target comparisons, including all twelve temperature regressors. ExtraTrees achieved the lowest observed temperature RMSE of 12.290 ∘C, representing a 5.54% reduction relative to its Temporal counterpart. Chemical-composition prediction also benefited from historical feedback, with particularly notable relative RMSE reductions for molybdenum (18.80%) and phosphorus (17.10%). The variation in leading regression algorithms across chemical elements further highlights the importance of combining a consistent information representation with target-specific predictive models.

The additional analyses provide further insights into the mechanisms and effectiveness of historical feedback. Feature-group ablation identified recent released outcomes and their moving statistical summaries as important sources of predictive information, while release-delay sensitivity experiments demonstrated the influence of feedback timeliness on prediction accuracy. In the retrospective later-period evaluation, adaptive residual correction reduced temperature RMSE from 12.502 to 12.275 ∘C (1.82%) without retraining the underlying regression model, with element-dependent responses for chemical composition. Comparisons with four DL architectures demonstrated the competitiveness of classical regressors equipped with engineered historical features, while target-specific SHAP analyses highlighted the complementary predictive contributions of historical outcomes and current-heat operational measurements.

Overall, the study establishes a systematic and reproducible methodology that integrates cutoff-aware industrial data processing, historical outcome availability, chronological model evaluation, and sequential residual feedback for EAF endpoint prediction. The findings demonstrate that improving the information available to predictive models can be as important as increasing model complexity. The proposed framework provides a foundation for adaptive, data-driven decision support in steelmaking, with potential applications in temperature management, chemical-composition monitoring, and process reliability. Future research will focus on prospective industrial validation, integration with actual measurement-release systems, and evaluation of the framework across additional EAF furnaces, production sites, and operating regimes to investigate its transferability and effectiveness in supporting operational decisions and process optimization.
